notes:
Passed on the fake backend by python3 -m mhs.driver check (evidence contract_checked, never an MHS-Device level). Model-authored and unreviewed; R1, so the loader does not refuse the hardware backend on review grounds, and this package claims no such protection. No hardware was attached, imported or run. DEVIATION FROM THE CARD: the card suggested PythonObjectDriver with cap.device.configure.v1 and cap.sensing.read.v1; cap.sensing.read.v1 binds sensor, sensor.imu and sensor.force_torque, not an instrument, so the settings are @read/@write state with cap.device.configure.v1 as the only catalogue binding, and measurement and auto setup are x-cap extensions over the DirectBackend object. NOT COVERED: the time and voltage sample arrays of read_waveform and auto_measure; the 0.9 catalogue has no oscilloscope waveform class. The scalar measure_waveform result and every setting are covered. The fake's read_waveform returns 8 samples and measure_waveform reports num_samples 8, while the real fetch defaults to 100000 samples (niscope_mcp/backends/direct.py:166-191); the fake is an in-memory stand-in, not a recording. Operator-required vertical_offset, trigger_level and record_length have no source bound in the clone; site-limits.example.json fills them for one example bench and the fake conformance run applies it. The driver takes bandwidth_filter, num_records, ref_position, enforce_realtime, acquisition_type, trigger_coupling and trigger_holdoff from backend options because get_current_config does not report them; their defaults are the upstream dataclass values, not sourced device limits. The vertical_range, probe_attenuation, input_impedance and sample_rate limits cite the clone's help-text cheat sheet of common values (niscope_mcp/__main__.py:1208-1214), the only text that states numbers; they are not datasheet limits.
